case_studies.went_wrong: Nudify tools were free and easy to use, most identified suspects were themselves minors, the platform cooperated little with police, and penalties were too weak to deter. Schools had no shared way to report or count cases.
case_studies.would_help: Laws that treat AI sexual images of children as child abuse material, including possession; a national tracking system and task force; a named response lead in every school; and teaching every pupil that a 'joke' deepfake is abuse.

case_studies.went_wrong: Boys aged 12 to 14 used a freely available app to turn girls' social media photos into nude images and shared them in group chats before any adult knew. Victims and parents had to push for action.
case_studies.would_help: A written school response plan, staff trained not to view or forward the images, fast removal through official channels, counselling for the girls from day one, and parents talking with children about nudify apps.

case_studies.went_wrong: A colleague cloned the principal's voice from public recordings and the fake clip spread online before anyone checked it. The principal faced threats while the school and police worked out that it was fake.
case_studies.would_help: Deepfake response plans that cover staff as well as pupils, a rule against impersonating anyone with AI, and verification before acting on a recording or message that seems to come from a school leader.

case_studies.went_wrong: The AI camera mistook a snack bag for a gun. District security cancelled the alert, but the principal did not know and passed it on, and armed police handcuffed the student.
case_studies.would_help: A trained person reviewing every alert before anyone acts on a pupil, a clear hand-off so a cancelled alert is known to everyone, and an impact assessment before such systems are installed.

case_studies.went_wrong: As alleged in the lawsuit, the chatbot kept engaging a 15-year-old on themes of death and did not alert anyone when he asked about suicide. Families and schools had little visibility of how he was using it.
case_studies.would_help: Age limits and approved, supervised tools at school, safety standards that require distress detection and signposting to human help, staff trained to spot reliance on chatbots, and AI literacy that teaches a chatbot is no substitute for a trusted adult.

case_studies.went_wrong: Questions were relayed out of exam halls to people using chatbots, and candidates copied the answers, sometimes including the chatbot's own error messages. Results were withheld at 235 schools.
case_studies.would_help: A clear ban on AI in national exams with secure, supervised conditions, malpractice rules that define AI misuse, and assessment designs that test key learning in the room.

case_studies.went_wrong: An AI monitoring tool collected screenshots of students' private writing about suicide, abuse and sexuality, and the links could be opened by anyone without a password. Some students were outed to school staff.
case_studies.would_help: A data protection impact assessment before buying monitoring tools, suppliers held to secure-by-default standards, and human review of every alert before action is taken.

measures.measure: Adopt a written response plan for sexual deepfakes of students or staff that names a senior lead (head or deputy) and sits inside your child-protection policy.
measures.why: Schools that act immediately and consistently limit spread and harm, and national regulators now publish step-by-step plans for this.

measures.measure: Do not view, copy, save, forward or delete a reported nude deepfake of a pupil yourself; pass it straight to the safeguarding lead.
measures.why: Making or holding indecent images of under-18s is illegal even when AI-generated, and handling them can retraumatise the child and destroy evidence.

measures.measure: Report suspected deepfake sexual abuse of a minor to police and child-protection services, meeting any mandatory reporting duty.
measures.why: Creating or sharing sexual images of children, real or synthetic, is a crime in many countries and regulators ask schools to report it.

measures.measure: Help victims get images taken down quickly using official removal routes (national online safety regulator, IWF/Childline Report Remove, NCMEC Take It Down, platform notices).
measures.why: Fast removal limits spread, and some laws now require platforms to remove reported images within 48 hours.

measures.measure: Give targeted students and staff counselling and wellbeing support from the first day, and tell parents early unless that would put the child at risk.
measures.why: Victims suffer serious harm, and guidance puts their wellbeing ahead of the investigation.

measures.measure: Teach every secondary pupil that making or sharing a 'nudified' or sexual deepfake of a classmate is abuse and can be a crime, even as a joke.
measures.why: Many perpetrators are pupils who do not realise the law applies to them.

measures.measure: Make sure national law treats AI-generated sexual images of children as child sexual abuse material and criminalises creating, acquiring, possessing and sharing them.
measures.why: UNICEF reports over a million children affected in one year and warns that the law has not caught up.

measures.measure: Set up national tracking of school deepfake incidents (victims, referrals, removals) with a task force that reviews cases regularly.
measures.why: South Korea's weekly tracking showed the true scale of the problem, including teacher victims, and drove referrals and removals.

measures.measure: Put deepfake abuse into the school behaviour and anti-bullying code with clear, proportionate sanctions up to exclusion.
measures.why: Clear consequences deter peer abuse, and some education systems now set expulsion as the top sanction.

measures.measure: Talk with children about nudify apps and deepfakes, and tell them they will not be blamed if they report being targeted.
measures.why: Children who fear blame stay silent, and guidance calls for safe reporting routes and family involvement.

measures.measure: Include school staff, not only pupils, in deepfake response plans, with support and removal help for teachers who are targeted.
measures.why: Teachers and other staff are also victims of sexual and defamatory deepfakes.

measures.measure: Require call-back verification on a known number before acting on any voice, video or message from a head, governor or official asking for money, passwords or data changes.
measures.why: AI voice clones and texts are being used to impersonate senior officials, and the voice alone can no longer be trusted.

measures.measure: Add AI-made phishing and impersonation emails to your risk assessment and to annual staff cyber training.
measures.why: GenAI makes scam emails that impersonate the school more believable.

measures.measure: Ban using AI to impersonate teachers, classmates or anyone else in the school's acceptable use policy.
measures.why: National classroom rules already prohibit deepfakes and impersonation by students.

measures.measure: Turn on multi-factor authentication for staff email, school social media and admin accounts so a cloned voice or stolen password alone cannot take them over.
measures.why: Impersonation campaigns aim to capture credentials, and MFA blocks most account takeovers.

measures.measure: Only let pupils use AI chatbots the school has approved, with age limits respected, supervision, and filtering and monitoring in place.
measures.why: Education guidance puts safety first and ties pupil use to these safeguards.

measures.measure: Set a national minimum age for independent GenAI use in school (13 is common) and require parental consent for older minors where appropriate.
measures.why: UNESCO recommends an age limit, and Gulf ministries have set 13 with supervision or parental consent rules.

measures.measure: Publish safety standards that any AI product sold to schools must meet: harmful-content filtering, logging, safeguarding alerts, distress detection and signposting to human help.
measures.why: England's product safety standards show how to make suppliers carry these duties.

measures.measure: Require education AI tools to avoid acting like a friend: no claims of feelings, no relationship-building, default time limits and flags for dependence.
measures.why: Emotional dependence on chatbots is a recognised harm and new supplier standards say products should avoid anthropomorphic, engagement-prolonging design.

measures.measure: Keep under-18s off social 'AI companion' apps and talk regularly about any chatbot your child uses.
measures.why: Independent testing found companions easily drew teens into sexual role-play and harmful advice, with weak age checks.

measures.measure: Train safeguarding staff to recognise signs that a pupil is relying on a chatbot for emotional support or discussing self-harm with it, and route those disclosures into normal safeguarding.
measures.why: Most companions tested failed to refer users to support services when suicide or self-harm came up.

measures.measure: Teach AI literacy: chatbots are not people, can be wrong, can be designed to keep you engaged, and are no substitute for a trusted adult.
measures.why: Psychologists and international frameworks call for AI literacy as a core protection for young people.

measures.measure: Use consumer, online-safety or child-protection regulators to demand evidence from chatbot companies on age checks and child-harm testing.
measures.why: Regulators in the US and Australia have compelled companies to explain how they protect children.

measures.measure: Prioritise the highest-impact controls first: MFA, patching known exploited flaws quickly, tested offline backups and a rehearsed incident response plan.
measures.why: These few measures stop most attacks on schools, which are frequent ransomware targets.

measures.measure: Never paste pupils' names, photos, grades, health or family details into a public AI tool.
measures.why: Data protection law applies, and guidance in England and the UAE says not to put personal data into GenAI.

measures.measure: Before buying any AI or edtech product, complete a data protection impact assessment and check that the supplier will not use pupil data to train models or for commercial purposes.
measures.why: Supplier standards require DPIAs and ban commercial reuse of children's data without a lawful basis.

measures.measure: Use collective purchasing power to require edtech suppliers to ship secure-by-default products with MFA and security fixes at no extra cost.
measures.why: Schools lack resources, so CISA urges pressing vendors to carry more of the security burden.

measures.measure: Join a sector information-sharing network and know in advance where to report a cyber incident.
measures.why: Shared threat intelligence and quick reporting help schools respond before damage spreads.

measures.measure: Set national minimum cyber security standards for schools, including annual risk assessments, MFA, patching deadlines and backups.
measures.why: England's standards give every school a clear baseline to meet and audit against.

measures.measure: Block unapproved AI platforms and VPN workarounds on school networks and devices.
measures.why: Unvetted tools can leak data, and national rules already prohibit them and filter bypassing.

measures.measure: Ban emotion-recognition AI in schools and universities except for genuine medical or safety reasons.
measures.why: The EU AI Act already prohibits it because such inferences are unreliable and intrusive.

measures.measure: Do not install facial recognition or other biometric systems without a prior impact assessment, DPO advice, consultation with families and explicit opt-in consent.
measures.why: A UK regulator reprimanded a school for skipping these steps, and New York has banned facial recognition in schools over misidentification risks.

measures.measure: Have a trained person review every alert from AI monitoring or safety software before any action is taken against a pupil.
measures.why: Automated alerts can be wrong, and safeguarding standards route alerts to humans rather than automatic sanctions.

measures.measure: Treat AI used for admissions, grading, placement or exam proctoring as high-risk, with human oversight, documentation and a route to appeal.
measures.why: The EU AI Act lists these education uses as high-risk because errors can change a student's life chances.

measures.measure: Never use an AI-text detector score as the sole evidence of cheating.
measures.why: Detectors are imperfect and have wrongly flagged most essays by non-native English writers as AI-written.

measures.measure: Check regularly that your filtering and monitoring systems cover generative AI tools pupils can reach.
measures.why: DfE guidance says filtering and monitoring should cover GenAI and points to statutory safeguarding guidance on keeping them appropriate.

measures.measure: Have a substantial share of coursework done in class under supervision, and check drafts as the work progresses.
measures.why: Teachers can then authenticate work with confidence rather than relying on detectors.

measures.measure: Use short conversations with students about their submitted work to confirm they understand and wrote it.
measures.why: A brief viva is one of the most reliable ways to check authorship when AI misuse is suspected.

measures.measure: Require students to acknowledge any AI use by naming the tool and date and keeping their prompts and outputs.
measures.why: Clear disclosure rules separate permitted help from malpractice.

measures.measure: Update the malpractice policy to define AI misuse and how it is handled, and explain it to students and parents.
measures.why: Exam boards require centres' policies to cover AI so that cases are handled fairly and consistently.

measures.measure: Redesign assessment so key learning outcomes are tested in secure, supervised conditions while other tasks openly allow AI.
measures.why: Quality agencies advise redesigning assessment rather than banning AI, and OECD finds AI-assisted gains can vanish in exams.

measures.measure: Ban AI use in formal national exams and keep a human responsible for every final mark even where AI assists marking.
measures.why: National rules and exam boards already require this to protect qualification integrity.

measures.measure: Publish a national framework for AI in education that sets out regulation, data protection and validation of tools, aligned to UNESCO guidance.
measures.why: UNESCO says most schools cannot vet AI tools alone and governments must set the framework.

measures.measure: Give every teacher training in AI ethics, safety and pedagogy using a competency framework.
measures.why: Teachers need these skills to judge tools and guide students, and frameworks set out what they should know.

measures.measure: Build AI literacy, including ethics, critical judgement and safe use, into the curriculum from primary school.
measures.why: International bodies and several Arab states now treat AI literacy as a core competence.

measures.measure: Tell parents which AI tools the school uses, what data they process, and seek agreement where required.
measures.why: Guidance says families should understand and agree to how pupils' data are processed by AI.

laws.what_it_does: Criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate images including AI deepfakes (up to three years' prison where the victim is a minor) and requires platforms to remove reported material within 48 hours from May 2026.

laws.law: Amendment to the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes (deepfake possession and viewing)
laws.what_it_does: Makes buying, saving, possessing or watching sexually explicit deepfakes punishable by up to three years in prison and raises the maximum for creating them to seven years.

laws.law: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 138 (Sexual Offences Act 2003 ss.66E-66H)
laws.what_it_does: Creates offences of creating, or requesting the creation of, sexual deepfakes of adults without consent, in force from 6 February 2026 (images of under-18s are already covered by indecent pseudo-photograph law).

laws.law: Crime and Policing Act 2026 (child sexual abuse image-generators)
laws.what_it_does: Makes it an offence to make, adapt, possess or supply tools such as AI models built to generate child sexual abuse images, with up to five years in prison; the Northern Ireland provision checked (s.73) was not yet in force.

laws.law: Indecent images of children law as applied in UKCIS guidance (pseudo-photographs)
laws.what_it_does: Official guidance confirms that making, possessing or sharing indecent AI-generated or manipulated images of under-18s is illegal, including when the maker is a child.

laws.law: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024 (No. 78, 2024)
laws.what_it_does: Creates a standalone federal offence of sharing sexual material of an adult without consent, expressly including material created or altered with technology such as deepfakes.

laws.law: Code pénal article 226-8-1 (inserted by Law No. 2024-449 'SREN' of 21 May 2024)
laws.what_it_does: Punishes sharing an AI-generated or edited sexual image or voice of a person without consent by up to two years and EUR 60,000, or three years and EUR 75,000 if shared online, even if labelled as fake.

laws.law: Law No. 132/2025 on artificial intelligence (Penal Code art. 612-quater)
laws.what_it_does: Makes spreading harmful AI-generated or altered images, video or voice without consent a crime punishable by one to five years, and requires parental consent for under-14s to use AI.
Prohibits AI systems that infer emotions of people in education institutions and workplaces, except for medical or safety reasons.

From 1 January 2026 requires companion chatbot operators to disclose they are AI, run suicide and self-harm protocols, give minors break reminders, and block sexually explicit chatbot images for minors.

sources.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
sources.summary: UNESCO's first global guidance on generative AI in education (published September 2023, page updated January 2026) asks governments to regulate GenAI tools and build coherent policy frameworks for education and research. It proposes an age limit for independent conversations with GenAI platforms, mandatory data-privacy protection, and an ethical validation process for tools because most schools cannot yet vet them.

sources.title: AI competency framework for students
sources.summary: Sets out 12 competencies across four dimensions (human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI techniques and applications, AI system design) at three levels: understand, apply, create. It is meant to help curricula prepare students to engage with AI safely and to exercise critical judgement of AI solutions.

sources.title: AI competency framework for teachers
sources.summary: Defines 15 competencies across five dimensions, including ethics of AI, AI pedagogy and AI for professional learning, at three levels: acquire, deepen, create. It is built on protecting teachers' rights and enhancing human agency, and gives strategies for putting ethical principles into practice.

sources.title: Guidance on AI and children, version 3.0
sources.summary: The December 2025 update of UNICEF's policy guidance sets ten requirements for child-centred AI, including regulatory oversight, child safety, protection of children's data and privacy, non-discrimination, transparency and accountability, and building children's AI skills. It comes with a checklist for governments and companies.

sources.title: 'Deepfake abuse is abuse' (statement)
sources.summary: UNICEF's 4 February 2026 statement cites UNICEF/ECPAT/INTERPOL research finding at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries had their images turned into sexual deepfakes in the past year. It calls on governments to bring AI-generated content into child sexual abuse material laws and criminalise its creation, acquisition, possession and sharing, and on AI firms to build in safety by design and prevent circulation.

sources.title: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026: Exploring effective uses of generative AI in education
sources.summary: Finds that general-purpose GenAI boosts task performance without real learning gains unless guided by pedagogy, and that students' advantage can disappear or reverse in exams once AI access is removed. It recommends purpose-built educational tools, equitable infrastructure and sustained professional learning (page blocked to direct fetch; content confirmed via search extract of the OECD page).

sources.title: Committee of Ministers recommendation on AI literacy
sources.summary: Recommendation to member states to help pupils, students, teachers, parents and citizens understand AI, use it responsibly and recognise where it threatens human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It gives effect to Article 20 of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (page blocked to direct fetch; content confirmed via search extract; exact adoption date not confirmed).

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 5 prohibited practices
sources.summary: Article 5(1)(f) bans placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that infer the emotions of people in workplaces and education institutions. The only exception is for systems intended for medical or safety reasons.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Annex III point 3 (education)
sources.summary: Classifies as high-risk AI used to decide admission or assignment to education, to evaluate learning outcomes, to assess the level of education a person will receive, and to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour by students during tests. High-risk systems carry obligations such as risk management, human oversight and documentation.

sources.title: Ethical guidelines on the use of AI and data in teaching and learning for educators (updated)
sources.summary: First issued in 2022 and updated in 2026 through the European Digital Education Hub, the guidelines explain the GDPR and AI Act context for teachers. They provide guiding questions and case examples for judging AI tools before using them in class.

sources.title: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education
sources.summary: DfE policy (updated August 2025) says safety should be the top priority, pupils should use GenAI only with safeguards such as supervision and filtering and monitoring, and personal data should not be put into GenAI tools. It warns GenAI can make cyber attacks and impersonation emails more credible and points to JCQ and Ofqual rules on AI malpractice.

sources.title: Generative AI: product safety standards
sources.summary: Standards for edtech suppliers (first issued January 2025, expanded 19 January 2026) covering filtering, monitoring and reporting to the safeguarding lead, security against jailbreaking, privacy, testing and governance. The 2026 update adds cognitive development, emotional and social development, mental health and anti-manipulation standards, including avoiding anthropomorphism and emotional dependence and detecting distress.

sources.title: Cyber security standards for schools and colleges
sources.summary: Sets standards including annual cyber risk assessment, staff and student training, MFA for staff cloud/remote and admin accounts, patching critical vulnerabilities within 14 days, and a 3-2-1 style backup plan. It also requires reporting cyber attacks internally and to bodies such as insurers and the DfE (last updated September 2026).

sources.organisation: UK Council for Internet Safety / DfE
sources.title: Sharing nudes and semi-nudes: advice for education settings working with children and young people
sources.summary: The March 2024 update explicitly covers AI-generated and digitally manipulated 'pseudo-images' of under-18s and says the law applies to children who make them. It tells staff to refer to the designated safeguarding lead, avoid viewing, copying or sharing images, refer to police or social care where needed, and use removal tools such as IWF/Childline Report Remove.

sources.title: Keeping children safe in education 2026
sources.summary: Statutory safeguarding guidance for schools and colleges, with the 2026 version in force from 1 September 2026. DfE's GenAI guidance names it as the core reference for online safety, filtering and monitoring and cyber security when schools use AI.

sources.title: AI Use in Assessments: Your role in protecting the integrity of qualifications
sources.country_or_scope: UK (GCSE, A level and other general qualifications)
sources.summary: Guidance effective 30 April 2025 treats AI misuse that leaves work not the student's own as malpractice and requires centres' malpractice policies to cover AI. It recommends supervised in-class work, checking drafts, short viva-style discussions and restricting AI on centre devices, says detectors must not be relied on alone, and says AI cannot be the sole marker.

sources.organisation: Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA)
sources.title: Maintaining quality and standards in the ChatGPT era: advice on generative AI tools
sources.summary: QAA advises universities that managed use of generative AI is preferable to outright bans, while maintaining academic standards. It offers a four-step process for identifying assessments that need adjusting and urges robust internal quality assurance.

sources.organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA)
sources.title: Enacting assessment reform in a time of artificial intelligence
sources.summary: Non-prescriptive TEQSA resource (released September 2025) that helps universities manage generative AI risks to the assurance of learning while teaching ethical use. It maps the main strategic pathways institutions are taking to redesign assessment (PDF timed out on direct fetch; description confirmed via search extracts).

sources.title: Essex school reprimanded after using facial recognition technology for canteen payments
sources.summary: The ICO reprimanded Chelmer Valley High School (23 July 2024) for introducing facial recognition without a data protection impact assessment, without consulting its DPO, parents or pupils, and relying on opt-out consent. It stresses a DPIA is required before biometric systems and that explicit opt-in consent is needed.

sources.title: Determination on biometric identifying technology in schools
sources.summary: The September 2023 determination bars New York schools from buying or using facial recognition technology, after a state report found the risks outweighed benefits, including higher misidentification rates for children and other groups. Other biometric tools are left to local decisions that must weigh privacy, civil rights, effectiveness and parental input (direct fetch failed on a certificate error; content confirmed via search extract of the NYSED release).

sources.organisation: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.title: Protecting Our Future: Partnering to Safeguard K-12 Organizations from Cybersecurity Threats
sources.summary: CISA's January 2023 report tells schools to start with the most impactful measures: MFA, patching known exploited vulnerabilities, tested backups, an exercised incident response plan and ongoing training. It also urges pressing vendors for secure-by-default products and joining information-sharing groups such as MS-ISAC and K12 SIX.

sources.title: Senior US Officials Impersonated in Malicious Messaging Campaign (PSA I-051525-PSA)
sources.summary: Warns that criminals are using AI-generated voice messages and texts to impersonate senior officials and steal account access. It advises verifying identity through a known number, not clicking links until verified, enabling two-factor authentication, using agreed code words, and confirming payment requests through a separate channel.

sources.title: FTC launches inquiry into AI chatbots acting as companions
sources.summary: On 11 September 2025 the FTC ordered seven firms, including Alphabet, Character.AI, Meta, OpenAI, Snap and xAI, to explain how they test, monitor and limit harms of companion chatbots to children. It asks about monetising engagement, age-restriction enforcement, disclosures to parents and use of conversation data.

sources.title: Toolkit for Schools: Guide to responding to image-based abuse involving AI deepfakes
sources.summary: Step-by-step guide (first released mid-2025, current PDF dated March 2026) for school leaders responding to nude or sexual deepfakes of students or staff, designed to sit alongside child-protection policies. eSafety urges schools to prioritise the wellbeing of targeted students and staff, report possible crimes to police, meet mandatory reporting duties and use eSafety for rapid removal (eSafety site blocked direct fetch; content confirmed via search extracts of the PDF and EducationHQ, 30 June 2025).

sources.title: Online safety advisory: AI chatbots and companions - risks to children and young people
sources.summary: The 18 February 2025 advisory warns that AI companions simulate personal relationships, allow unregulated discussion of sex, self-harm and suicide, and often lack effective age checks. eSafety later issued legal notices (October 2025) to Character.AI, Nomi, Chai and Chub AI and reported that most companions failed to refer users to support for suicide or self-harm (confirmed via Digital Policy Alert and search extracts; eSafety site blocked direct fetch).

sources.organisation: Republic of Korea Ministry of Education (reported by The Korea Herald)
sources.title: Education Ministry response to school deepfake sex crimes
sources.summary: In August 2024 the ministry set up an emergency task force to track school deepfake cases weekly, handle victim reports, give psychological support and strengthen digital-ethics education. It said high-school perpetrators could face expulsion, the top sanction in the school-violence system.

sources.organisation: Republic of Korea Ministry of Education (reported by The Korea Times)
sources.title: 799 students, 31 teachers victimized by deepfake videos this year
sources.summary: Ministry survey data showed 833 school victims of deepfakes in 2024 to late October, including 799 students and 31 teachers. Schools referred 417 cases for investigation and 218 for deletion of videos.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being: An APA Health Advisory
sources.summary: June 2025 advisory saying adolescents need special protections from AI because of developmental stage. Its recommendations cover healthy boundaries with simulated relationships, privacy, protecting young people's likenesses and AI literacy.

sources.title: AI Companions Decoded: risk assessment of social AI companions
sources.summary: April 2025 risk assessment, done with Stanford's Brainstorm lab, concluding that social AI companions pose unacceptable risks and that under-18s should not use them. It calls for age assurance beyond self-declaration and scrutiny of manipulative relationship patterns and emotional dependency.

sources.organisation: Stanford University researchers (Liang et al.), published in Patterns
sources.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed study finding widely used AI-text detectors frequently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated while classifying native writing correctly. The authors caution against using such detectors in evaluative or educational settings.

sources.organisation: Ireland Department of Education and Youth
sources.title: Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Schools
sources.summary: National guidance published 21 October 2025 with Oide to help schools plan safe, ethical and appropriate AI use, drawing on UNESCO and EU work. It notes the State Examinations Commission requires AI-generated material to be referenced, and a taskforce on AI in education including assessment was announced (gov.ie blocked direct fetch; confirmed via search extracts of gov.ie and Eurydice).

sources.organisation: UAE Ministry of Education (reported by Education Middle East)
sources.title: Safe and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms (manual)
sources.summary: The 2026 manual bans generative AI for students under 13 or below Year 7, bans AI in formal exams and undisclosed AI work, and prohibits entering personal data of students, teachers or parents into AI tools. It also prohibits deepfakes and impersonation and requires direct teacher oversight of classroom AI use.

sources.organisation: Saudi Ministry of Education and SDAIA (reported by Gulf News)
sources.title: Guidelines for using generative AI in education
sources.summary: Joint guidebook for students, teachers and parents aimed at ethical and responsible use that keeps the teacher central. It says students under 13 should not use GenAI without direct supervision and under-18s need clear parental consent.

sources.organisation: Center for Educational Research and Development (CRDP), Lebanon
sources.title: Lebanon's AI Competency Framework / AI Educational Framework for students and teachers
sources.summary: CRDP, which develops Lebanon's national curriculum, published (October 2025) an AI framework whose first part is an AI policy for Lebanese schools built on UNESCO's 2024 frameworks and 2021 AI ethics recommendation. Its guiding principles include a human-centred approach, data privacy and security, inclusivity and teacher professional development (PDF text could not be extracted locally; content confirmed via search extract of the PDF).

sources.organisation: Egypt Ministry of Education and Technical Education (reported by Egyptian Streets)
sources.title: AI curricula in schools from 2025-2026
sources.summary: The minister announced AI curricula in selected primary, preparatory and secondary grades from 2025-26, including the ethics and social implications of AI. No published usage or safeguarding guideline from the ministry was found.

sources.title: SB 243 companion chatbot law
sources.summary: Signed 13 October 2025 and effective 1 January 2026, SB 243 requires companion chatbot operators to disclose that users are talking to AI, keep suicide and self-harm protocols, and report crisis-referral data to the state health department. For minors it requires break reminders and blocks sexually explicit images generated by the chatbot.

sources.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
sources.summary: Federal law signed 19 May 2025 that criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate images, including AI deepfakes, with up to three years in prison where the victim is a minor. Covered platforms had until 19 May 2026 to set up a process to remove reported material within 48 hours.

sources.title: Draft Organic Law for the protection of minors in digital environments
sources.summary: Bill approved by the Council of Ministers in March 2025 that would reform the Penal Code to criminalise sexual deepfakes and grooming and add bans from digital environments as a penalty. Final enactment could not be confirmed (search extract only).
